Neonates of the Ocellated lizard (Timon lepidus) emerge from their parchment-shelled eggs with a snout-vent length of approximately 2.6 centimeters [Lb = approximately 2.6 centimeters], a measurement that reflects the substantial yolk reserves provisioned during embryonic development. This relatively large hatchling size is characteristic of many lacertid lizards and confers advantages in foraging and predator avoidance from the moment of eclosion. Following emergence, these young individuals undergo a period of rapid somatic growth, gradually increasing in body length until they approach the asymptotic size typical of their population. Adults of this species ultimately reach a snout-vent length of about 21 centimeters [Li = about 21 centimeters], a value that places Timon lepidus among the larger-bodied members of its genus. Field surveys conducted across the Iberian Peninsula have documented that adults attaining this maximum size are typically older individuals with well-established territories, suggesting that growth rates may decelerate considerably after sexual maturation.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], females of Timon lepidus exhibit a maximum reproductive output of 21 eggs per season [Ri = 21 eggs per season], with the capacity to produce a single clutch annually [F_R_i = single clutch annually]. This seasonal fecundity, which represents the upper bound of reproductive potential for the species, is likely constrained by the energetic demands of vitellogenesis and the finite duration of the active period in Mediterranean climates. Gravid females are known to select nest sites with specific thermal regimes to optimize incubation conditions, and clutch size can vary considerably depending on maternal body condition and resource availability in the preceding months. The eggs themselves are leathery-shelled and undergo a developmental period that depends strongly on ambient temperature, with cooler conditions prolonging the incubation interval and potentially affecting hatchling phenotypes. Comparisons with other lacertids of comparable body size indicate that this level of annual egg production is typical for a lizard investing heavily in relatively large offspring.

Mark-recapture studies conducted over several decades have provided robust estimates of longevity for Timon lepidus under natural conditions. When maintained at a stable thermal environment of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the maximum lifespan recorded for this species extends to approximately 17 years [am = approximately 17 years], a duration that distinguishes it as one of the longer-lived European lacertids. This extended lifespan is thought to be linked to a relatively slow pace of life, characterized by delayed maturity and modest annual reproductive effort compared to smaller, more short-lived congeners. Senescence in older individuals manifests as a gradual decline in locomotor performance and a reduction in reproductive output, although some females have been observed to produce clutches well into their second decade of life. The ability to persist for such a lengthy period likely reflects a combination of low predation pressure in certain habitats and an efficient physiological capacity for tissue maintenance and repair. These longevity data are critical for constructing accurate demographic models and understanding population dynamics in the face of environmental change.

Roughly 2.5 years [tR = Roughly 2.5 years] after its own hatching, at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], Timon lepidus initiates its first breeding event, a key life-history transition. This relatively extended juvenile phase is consistent with the species' large body size and its investment in reaching a threshold mass before allocating resources to gonadal development and egg production. During this pre-reproductive period, hatchlings must accumulate sufficient lipid reserves and somatic tissue to support the energetic costs of reproduction, a process that may be delayed by suboptimal environmental conditions or limited prey availability. The onset of first reproduction is typically marked by the emergence of distinctive breeding coloration in males and the enlargement of ovarian follicles in females, events that are tightly coordinated with the seasonal availability of food resources and favorable thermal conditions. Individuals that attain this milestone earlier in life may enjoy a longer reproductive lifespan, but they may also incur trade-offs in terms of reduced growth or future fecundity.

As adults, reproductively active females of Timon lepidus attain a maximum wet body weight of approximately 549.98 grams [Wwi = approximately 549.98 grams], a mass that correlates strongly with snout-vent length and reflects the substantial pelvic volume required to accommodate a full complement of developing eggs. This ultimate body mass is achieved only after several years of growth, and individuals that reach this size are typically dominant within their local populations, commanding prime basking sites and foraging territories. The gravid condition imposes considerable locomotor costs, and pregnant females often exhibit reduced sprint speeds, which may elevate their vulnerability to predators during the nesting period. Nonetheless, the energetic benefits of larger body size, including higher fecundity and improved competitive ability, appear to outweigh these risks in most habitats occupied by the species. Comparative analyses across lacertid lizards indicate that the wet mass of adult Timon lepidus is among the highest recorded for the family, underscoring the species' position as a large-bodied, slow-living reptile in Mediterranean ecosystems.
